outcome: No accepted proof, disproof or counterexample of Lemoine's conjecture has appeared since 26 January 2024. The in-window activity is (a) two Lean-checked, AI-generated proofs in the OEIS Open benchmark paper (arXiv:2608.11941, 12 Aug 2026) that establish Lemoine's conjecture only conditionally, on two open Sun conjectures; (b) a GitHub repository (first commit 30 Apr 2026) claiming a 'constructive' machine-verified proof, whose Lean files as I could read them declare no theorem; and (c) asymptotic-only revisions of the Agama–Gensel preprint arXiv:1709.05335, whose full-conjecture claim (first on this identifier in March 2021) was conditional by the author's own comment and was reframed as asymptotic in November 2023.
problem_asks: Whether every odd integer n greater than 5 can be written as n = p + s, where p is an odd prime and s is an even semiprime. An even semiprime is 2q with q prime, so the statement is equivalent to: for every odd n > 5 there exist primes p and q with n = p + 2q (p and q need not be distinct). Parts: (1) the quantifier ranges over all odd n > 5, so the claim is unbounded; (2) for each such n an odd prime p must exist; (3) the remainder n − p must be twice a prime. It asks for existence only: no bound, no count of representations, no construction and no asymptotic form is asked for.

events.what_happened: Zsófia Juhász, Máté Bartalos, Péter Magyar and Gábor Farkas, 'Empirical verification of a new generalisation of Goldbach's conjecture up to 10^12 (or 10^13) for all coefficients ≤ 40', arXiv:2304.00024. The abstract states that Lemoine's conjecture is verified up to a new record of 10^13 (the journal abstract reads: 'We verify Lemoine's conjecture up to a new record of 10^13'). Journal version: Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.4.3, published 18 Mar 2024. The paper does not claim a proof of Lemoine's conjecture.

events.delivers: Lemoine's conjecture holds for every odd n up to 10^13 (computation; no counterexample reported). This is a finite check of a universal claim and, under the scope rule in §2.1, moves nothing about the conjecture.
events.remains: Every odd n above 10^13, which is all of the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama and Berndt Gensel, 'Studies in Additive Number Theory by Circles of Partition', arXiv:2012.01329 (v1 2 Dec 2020). The abstract, as I read it, says the paper 'finishes by presenting an asymptotic proof of the binary Goldbach and Lemoine conjecture' as an application of the circle embedding method. I did not read the body.
events.revisions: Comment on the arXiv page: '58 pages; the paper has been massively reformatted and introduction expanded;' and 'a visual of the structure of circle of partitions has been supplied'. Later versions not read.
events.delivers: Per the abstract only: an asymptotic statement (sufficiently large odd n) for Lemoine's conjecture. It does not establish the all-n statement.
events.remains: The all-n statement, and whatever finite range the asymptotic argument does not cover.
events.doubts: The body was not read, so I cannot assess the argument. The same authors' later preprint arXiv:1709.05335 (see the 2021 event) contains an author comment that a key lemma was wrong at v6. I did not check whether this 2020 preprint has the same gap.
events.direction: Asymptotic claim (sufficiently large n). It cuts toward the conjecture only for almost all odd n.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama and Berndt Gensel, arXiv:1709.05335. The Lemoine argument first appears on this identifier in v3 (2 Mar 2021), titled 'A Proof of Lemoine's Conjecture by Circles of Partition'. Its abstract says: 'we show by using the notion of circles of partition that for all odd numbers n≥9 holds' n = p + 2q with p, q primes not necessarily distinct, and that the method proves the Lemoine conjecture. The identifier's arXiv date is 12 Sep 2017, but v1 and v2 (Sep 2017) carry a different title and abstract, 'On elementary estimates for sum of some functions in certain arithmetic progressions' by the same author, with no Lemoine content. So the first Lemoine content on this identifier is March 2021. Wikipedia dates the claim to 2017 and says: 'A proof was claimed in 2017 by Agama and Gensel, but this was later found to be flawed', citing v6. In v9 (28 Nov 2023) the title became 'The Asymptotic Binary Goldbach and Lemoine Conjectures' and the abstract says the aim is 'to prove the binary Goldbach as well as the Lemoine conjecture', with asymptotic versions proved by the method.
events.revisions: v1 12 Sep 2017 and v2 18 Sep 2017 (different paper, 'On elementary estimates…'). v3 2 Mar 2021 (first Lemoine content, 7 pages). v4 11 Mar 2021; v5 12 Mar 2021 (dates from the version table; contents not read). v6 21 Mar 2021, comment: 'The first proof of the Little Lemma was wrong and still under construction. So the current proof is conditional and will be completed!!'. v7 13 Dec 2021; v8 19 Aug 2023 (contents not read). v9 28 Nov 2023: title and abstract changed to asymptotic versions; comment includes 'It fixes the little lemma in the previous version and provides asymptotic results.' v10 10 Jan 2024 (contents not read). v11 28 Jun 2024: comment 'Note: This is not a new submission on the study of Lemoine and the binary Goldbach conjecture.', plus the same 'fixes the little lemma' sentence. v12 10 Jul 2024. v13 14 Mar 2026, v14 4 Apr 2026, v15 13 Apr 2026, v16 19 Apr 2026 (current). The 2026 comments say the paper was reformatted, the introduction greatly expanded and 'ideas remain unchanged'. No 2026 revision I read adds a full-conjecture claim.
events.delivers: As claimed in the v3 and v6 abstracts: the full conjecture for all odd n ≥ 9. The author's own v6 comment says the Little Lemma was not yet proved, so the claim is conditional on it. I could not read the v3–v6 text, so I cannot say which steps depend on the lemma beyond the comment.
events.remains: The full conjecture as claimed, because the author's own comment says the key lemma was unproved at v6 and no version I read restores an unconditional full-conjecture claim. From v9 the paper claims only asymptotic results.
events.time_since_posted: 5 years 7 months since v3 (2 Mar 2021) to 13 Oct 2026; 2 years 10 months since the asymptotic-only version (v9, 28 Nov 2023)
events.directly_checkable: Each odd n can be checked by hand for a representation. The general claim cannot be checked this way.
events.doubts: (1) The author's own v6 comment: 'The first proof of the Little Lemma was wrong and still under construction. So the current proof is conditional and will be completed!!' (2) Wikipedia says the 2017 claim 'was later found to be flawed', citing v6. The Wikipedia text I read does not describe the flaw or name who found it, and I found no other public statement of a flaw. (3) The author reframed the result as asymptotic in v9 (28 Nov 2023), and the full-conjecture claim was not carried forward. (4) In v16 the asymptotic Theorem 5.4 rests on a conditional Theorem 3.8 whose hypothesis is stated for all t ≥ 4. The text as I read it says the hypotheses are 'asymptotically fulfilled', and I did not verify that step. This is a reading of the 2026 version, not of the 2021 argument.

withdrawn.what: No withdrawal found. The full-conjecture claim was dropped in place: v9 changed the title and abstract to asymptotic versions, and the v9 and v11 comments say the change fixes the little lemma and provides asymptotic results.

events.direction: Claimed proof in the conjecture's direction (every odd n ≥ 9 is p + 2q), conditional by the author's own comment at v6. From v9 the claimed scope is asymptotic only.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama and Berndt Gensel, 'Complex Circles of Partition and the Asymptotic Lemoine Conjecture', AfricArXiv preprint (DOI 10.14293/111.000/000049.v1; also 10.60763/africarxiv/1305). The abstract says: 'With it we can prove an asymptotic version of the Lemoine Conjecture.' The repository gives the issue date as 13 Oct 2022 and an accession date of 25 Mar 2024.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'A progress on the binary Goldbach conjecture', arXiv:1706.09803 (v1 26 Jun 2017; v9 13 Mar 2026). The v9 abstract says: 'As an application we prove conditionally the binary Goldbach conjecture'; 'We develop a series of steps to prove the binary Goldbach conjecture in full'; and 'We end the paper by proving the binary Goldbach conjecture for all sufficiently large even numbers.' This is a neighbouring problem, not Lemoine's conjecture. Lemoine's conjecture implies the ternary Goldbach statement, not the binary one, so this paper does not bear on Lemoine. Recorded here as a discounted neighbour.
events.revisions: v9 13 Mar 2026 (comment: '20 pages; the paper has been reformatted and introduction expanded; ideas remain unchanged'). The v1 contents were not read; the date is the arXiv v1 submission date.
events.delivers: Binary Goldbach, a different question. Per v9, a conditional proof and a proof for sufficiently large even numbers. Under §2.1 it settles nothing about Lemoine's conjecture.
events.remains: Not applicable to Lemoine's conjecture: this event does not address it.
events.direction: Binary Goldbach (a different conjecture); conditional and large-n claims in v9. Not a result on Lemoine's conjecture.

events.what_happened: GitHub repository AEjonanonymous/Lemoine-Conjecture, described as 'A Machine-Verified Constructive Proof of Lemoine's Conjecture', CC BY 4.0. The README, titled 'The Lemoine Predictive Theorem', names the author as Jonathan f(n) Reed (an ORCID is given on the page). It claims: 'a valid prime partition for any odd integer N > 5 is logically guaranteed' and 'Constructive proof of Lemoine's Conjecture via a guided logical chain'. The two Lean files, lemoine_predictive_theorem.lean (858 bytes) and lemoine_generalized_theorem.lean (552 bytes), as read through my tools, define get_next_key and lemoine_search (predictive) and get_reservoir and lemoine_search (generalised), with termination_by on list length. Neither file declares a theorem, lemma or example, and neither contains a statement connecting the code to Lemoine's conjecture. The repository also holds a PDF manuscript (204,962 bytes), which I could not read. The GitHub topic mirror lists the repository with 1 star.
events.revisions: 21 commits. 30 Apr 2026 'Initial commit'; 1 May 2026 many README edits and file uploads (including deleting and re-adding the PDF); 19 May 2026 LICENSE; 25 May 2026 lean-toolchain and lakefile.lean; 18 Jul 2026 'Update lakefile.lean' (latest). All commits by AEjonanonymous.
events.delivers: As I read the files: no statement about Lemoine's conjecture is established in Lean. The code defines a search that, if it returns a nonzero value, gives a decomposition N = (N − 2·p) + 2·p with both parts prime. Nothing in the files proves that the search returns a nonzero value for every odd N > 5, and that claim is the conjecture.
events.remains: All of the conjecture. Nothing in the files shows the search returns a nonzero value for every odd N > 5.
events.time_since_posted: 5 months since the initial commit (to 13 Oct 2026)

events.what_happened: Tom Adamczewski, arXiv:2608.11941, 'OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?' (v1 12 Aug 2026; v2 13 Aug 2026; 26 pages). The results table and Appendix A list OEIS A236566 as 'Proved', with a dollar figure of $3. A236566 is Zhi-Wei Sun's conjecture (OEIS, 28 Jan 2014). Part (i): a(n) > 0 for all n > 2, which OEIS says implies Goldbach and twin primes. Part (ii): for n > 30, 2n + 1 = 2p + q with p, q and prime(p + 2) + 2 all prime, which OEIS says implies Lemoine's conjecture and the twin prime conjecture. The Lean theorem in the benchmark results repository (oeis_236566_conjecture_2) reads: theorem oeis_236566_conjecture_2 : a236566_conjecture_part_ii → lemoine_conjecture ∧ twin_prime_conjecture. So the formal proof establishes Lemoine's conjecture only from part (ii). The appendix's proof summary reads: 'For Lemoine's conjecture, swap the two primes in the asserted representation for large odd integers and check the finitely many smaller cases explicitly.' The OEIS entry for A236566 (comment by Michael De Vlieger, 19 Aug 2026) points to the paper's proof abstract without stating a check.
events.revisions: v2 13 Aug 2026. The OEIS comment linking the paper is dated 19 Aug 2026.
events.delivers: A Lean-checked implication: if part (ii) holds (for all n > 30, some prime p with prime(p + 2) + 2 prime gives 2n + 1 − 2p prime), then every odd k > 5 is p + 2q with p, q prime, and twin primes are infinite. The Lemoine conclusion, in the formal statement, matches the usual one (odd k > 5, primes p and q). The row proves that implication, not the conjecture.
events.remains: Part (ii), which is an open conjecture. Lemoine's conjecture for all odd k > 5 is unestablished unless part (ii) is established; the twin prime conclusion is likewise conditional.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4; checker SafeVerify. The paper's §2.3 says a submission is accepted only if it passes SafeVerify. The results repository says runs before the switch to Comparator were checked by SafeVerify.
machine_checked.sorry_free: No sorry, axiom, native_decide or admit seen in the raw Spec.lean as I fetched it. Not compiled by me.

events.directly_checkable: The formal hypothesis a236566_conjecture_part_ii is a universal statement over n > 30 with an explicit prime condition, and could in principle be tested for each n. The Lean proof of the implication was not checked by me.
events.doubts: (1) The Lean theorem assumes part (ii). The 'Proved' label means the implication was proved; the hypothesis is not established by anything I found. (2) The same proof summary extends the argument to the twin prime conjecture from the same hypothesis, and twin primes are open. The row therefore claims only the implication. (3) The paper's own limitation (§4.1): 'We have taken the Tsoukalas dataset as-is without performing further validation' and 'It seems likely that at least some conjectures are misformalized.' (4) On the seqfan thread (24 Aug 2026), Antti Karttunen reports that a claimed disproof of A379240 in the same benchmark is false, because the agent confused A376418 with A129251, and asks readers to check claimed results manually. (5) The OEIS comment of 19 Aug 2026 points to the paper's proof abstract and states no verification.
events.direction: Cuts toward Lemoine's conjecture in its own direction, but only as a conditional implication from part (ii). The formal theorem is an implication, not Lemoine's conjecture itself.
people: Tom Adamczewski (paper and benchmark author; no individual proof credit given in the paper)

events.what_happened: Same paper, arXiv:2608.11941. The results table and Appendix A list OEIS A219055 as 'Proved', with a dollar figure of $4. A219055 is Zhi-Wei Sun's conjecture (OEIS, 11 Nov 2012). Its comment states: if a(n) > 0 for every even n > 8012 and every odd n > 15727, then Goldbach's conjecture, Lemoine's conjecture and the conjecture that there are infinitely many primes p with p + 6 also prime all hold. The Lean theorem in the results repository (oeis_219055_conjecture_1) reads: theorem oeis_219055_conjecture_1 : a219055_core_conjecture → goldbach_conjecture ∧ lemoine_conjecture ∧ six_prime_gap_conjecture. The core conjecture is defined as ∀ n, ((Even n ∧ 8012 < n) ∨ (Odd n ∧ 15727 < n)) → A219055 n > 0. The appendix's proof summary: 'The finite Goldbach and Lemoine ranges are certified using explicit witness lists and a proved-correct Boolean trial-division primality checker', with positivity above the thresholds yielding a witness.
events.delivers: A Lean-checked implication: if the core positivity claim (A219055(n) > 0 for all even n > 8012 and odd n > 15727) holds, then Goldbach's conjecture, Lemoine's conjecture and the infinitude of primes p with p + 6 prime hold. The Lemoine conclusion in the formal statement is for every odd n ≥ 7 with a representation n = p + 2q. It includes the finite check of small cases. The row proves the implication, not Lemoine's conjecture.
events.remains: The core positivity claim, which is an open statement and is the antecedent of the implication. Lemoine's conjecture for all odd n is unestablished unless the core is established. The Goldbach and six-prime-gap conclusions are likewise conditional.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4; checker SafeVerify. The paper's §2.3 says a submission is accepted only if it passes SafeVerify. The results repository says runs before the switch to Comparator were checked by SafeVerify.

events.directly_checkable: The core positivity hypothesis is an explicit computable inequality for each n, so instances can be tested by hand. The finite Lemoine and Goldbach checks are in the Lean file. I did not run them.
events.doubts: (1) The Lean theorem assumes the core positivity claim. Nothing I read proves it. (2) The conclusion includes the infinitude of primes p with p + 6 prime, which is the open cousin-prime question; the implication does not settle it. (3) The paper's limitation (§4.1) applies here as for A236566: the Tsoukalas formalisations were used as-is and 'it seems likely that at least some conjectures are misformalized'. (4) On the seqfan thread, Karttunen warns that a claimed disproof of A379240 in the same benchmark is false and asks for manual checks. (5) The OEIS comment (Michael De Vlieger, 19 Aug 2026) points to the paper's proof abstract and states no verification.
events.direction: Cuts toward Lemoine's conjecture in its direction, but only as a conditional implication from the core positivity claim. The formal theorem is an implication, not Lemoine's conjecture itself.

disputes.summary: Naming: the conjecture was first stated by Émile Lemoine (L'intermédiaire des mathématiciens, 1894–1896). MathWorld erroneously credited Hyman Levy (Math. Gaz. 1963), so 'Levy's conjecture' persists as a name. Wikipedia and OEIS A046927 both record this.

Agama and Gensel: the 2021 claim (v3–v6) says all odd n ≥ 9 are p + 2q. The author's v6 comment says the Little Lemma was wrong and the proof is conditional. Wikipedia says the claim 'was later found to be flawed' with no flaw described in the text I read. From v9 (28 Nov 2023) the paper claims only asymptotic results.

AEjonanonymous's repository calls itself a 'Machine-Verified Constructive Proof of Lemoine's Conjecture'. The two .lean files as I read them declare no theorem, only a search function, and the README claims a proof.

The OEIS Open table marks A236566 and A219055 'Proved', while the Lean theorems proved are implications from open conjectures (part (ii) of A236566; the core positivity claim of A219055). The paper's own text and the OEIS comments describe the rows as conjectures and implications.

summary: Across 33 searches and roughly 60 opened or attempted sources, I found no accepted proof, disproof or counterexample of Lemoine's conjecture since 26 January 2024, and no AI system credited with the conjecture itself. Three things bear on the window. (1) On 12 Aug 2026 Tom Adamczewski's OEIS Open paper (arXiv:2608.11941) marks OEIS A219055 and A236566 as 'Proved'. Both are Sun conjectures whose Lean proofs, in the benchmark's results repository, prove Lemoine's conjecture only as an implication: A236566 from its part (ii), and A219055 from its core positivity claim. The per-sample records attribute the A219055 proof to Claude Fable 5 and the A236566 proof to Claude Opus 4.8, but the paper's prose does not name the model for either row, so the attribution rests on the results repository. This is the closest call: a reader could take the 'Proved' label as a resolution, but the formal theorems assume open statements, and the paper says the formalisations were used unchecked and that some are likely misformalized. (2) A GitHub repository (AEjonanonymous/Lemoine-Conjecture, first commit 30 Apr 2026) calls itself a constructive, machine-verified proof. Its two .lean files, as I could read them, define a search function and declare no theorem; the PDF manuscript was not readable, and I did not compile the project. (3) Agama and Gensel's arXiv:1709.05335 is dated 2017 by its identifier and by Wikipedia, but its Lemoine content first appears in v3 (2 Mar 2021), which claims all odd n ≥ 9 with a Little Lemma that the author's own v6 comment says was unproved. From v9 (Nov 2023) the paper claims asymptotic results only; 2026 revisions v13–v16 are reformatting. Before the window, Juhász et al. verified Lemoine up to 10^13 (arXiv 31 Mar 2023; JIS 2024), a finite check. No other Lemoine event, human or AI, surfaced. Searches for Formal Conjectures, Lean Zulip, MathOverflow and zbMATH did not reach relevant material. The same OEIS Open table also marks A001359 (twin primes) 'Proved' ($5). That is a neighbouring famous problem and is not recorded as an event here, but it is further reason to check the table's labels.
competing_reading: For counting Lemoine's conjecture as touched by AI in this window: two Lean-checked, AI-generated proofs are in an accepted set, the paper presents them as 'Proved', and each formal theorem's conclusion is Lemoine's statement. Against: each formal theorem assumes an open statement, so the record contains no unconditional result, and the formal statements are unvalidated. On dating: Wikipedia and the arXiv identifier put the Agama–Gensel claim in 2017; the first Lemoine content on that identifier is March 2021. Either date leaves the claim unaccepted, so the choice does not change the status.
what_would_settle_it: (a) A Lean or human-checked proof of the A219055 core positivity claim or of A236566 part (ii); either would make the corresponding implication unconditional. (b) A check that the Tsoukalas formal statements for A219055 and A236566 faithfully match Sun's conjectures. (c) A compile of the AEjonanonymous .lean files showing a theorem whose statement is Lemoine's conjecture with no sorry or extra axioms, plus the PDF manuscript's text. (d) The v3–v6 full text of arXiv:1709.05335 for the Little Lemma, and any journal, zbMATH or MathSciNet record of the Agama–Gensel argument. (e) The source for Wikipedia's 'later found to be flawed', including who found the flaw and where it was stated.
